sessions.title: Who Keeps It Open?
sessions.description:
Every generational shift in computing produces plumbing that everyone depends on. TCP/IP, HTTP, the container runtime. And every time, there is a window where someone can quietly come to own it, and everyone else pays rent. The plumbing for AI agents is in that window right now.

This talk is about why it matters. Why “open” is a present-tense word, decided one release at a time unless neutral governance makes it permanent. Why the agentic layer captures something bigger than social media ever did, why a protocol owned by one vendor is just private property and you can get kicked out. 

And why the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) is that neutral home for the agentic stack, which will guarantee openness, transparency, and access, and why over 300 companies have joined the AAIF to help further this mission.

sessions.title: End to End Software Development Lifecycle Hardening with AMPEL
sessions.description:
As software delivery accelerates, teams need automated ways to verify compliance and security controls across the SDLC.

Hardening a pipeline means checking many things: who can run CI, whether repositories are configured safely, cryptographically verifying commit authors, whether tools and build chains have trusted provenance, auditing for vulnerabilities, and if all this is acceptable before release.

Yes there's a tool for each step, but stitching them together quickly becomes an unmaintainable mess.

Enter AMPEL, the supply chain policy engine. AMPEL uses policy as code to evaluate each stage of the SDLC, blocking builds when conditions are not met. Uniform, reusable policies help protect your systems, users, and organization from insecure releases.

In this hands-on session, we’ll use community-driven policies to lock down steps, monitor checks, and map controls to frameworks like the OSPS Baseline and NIST SSDF. Bring a project and a laptop; let’s harden it together.

sessions.title: MCP Without Polling: Building Reactive Agents with Continuous Queries
sessions.description:
Polling current state forces agents to trade freshness for repeated queries and can miss conditions that appear and disappear between checks. Forwarding every raw change makes models spend expensive tokens deciding which events matter.

This session shows MCP developers and agent builders how continuous graph queries in Drasi turn changes in existing data sources into streams of meaningful business events. Examples include orders becoming high-value and orders remaining unprocessed beyond a deadline, even when no new database write occurs.

The demo follows an agent discovering streams, choosing a subscription, and using MCP tools to investigate and act when a relevant event arrives. A prototype of MCP's emerging Events extension, a proposed standard for event discovery and subscriptions, connects producers and agents.

Attendees will learn to separate event detection from agent reasoning, understand query-result transitions, and combine event subscriptions with authoritative tool calls.

sessions.title: Creating VEX Documents at Scale: A Look into One Supplier's Process
sessions.description:
What is a VEX? What goes into it? How should you determine that? When and how should you create one? Why do you need one? This session answers those questions and more through a case study into how a large software supplier, Microsoft, is preparing to automate the creation of VEX documents. Specifically, the CSAF VEX specification required fields and options will be covered, however OpenVEX will also be investigated. 

VEX documents are now a vital necessity for secure usage and inclusion of Open Source Software. They are required to supply software in compliance with EU CRA, alongside SBOM. With AI accelerating the rate of discovery of security vulnerabilities, VEX documents will be more and more applicable, as software suppliers will have trouble keeping up and many vulnerabilities are not exploitable.

sessions.title: Agents Will Be Judged on Where They Run
sessions.description:
The agent ecosystem has grown up assuming a hosted frontier model and an outbound connection. That assumption is fine for a lot of use cases and disqualifying for a lot of others: regulated industries, public sector, anywhere data residency or air-gapped operation is the starting condition rather than an edge case.


Those constraints aren't going away, and the capability gap that made them painful is closing fast as open-weight models get good enough for scoped, tool-using work. This talk argues that placement is about to become a first-class design concern for agentic systems, not a deployment afterthought, and looks at what has to be true of the runtime for an agent loop to work with no egress: local tool access, local audit, local identity, and a lifecycle you can operate across sites you can't reach.

sessions.title: MCP Is the New Internal API Surface
sessions.description:
MCP makes it radically easier to expose tools, data, and actions to agents. That’s great. It also means organizations are about to create a lot of MCP servers.

We’ve seen this pattern before with internal APIs: rapid adoption, duplicated capabilities, unclear ownership, inconsistent standards, stale interfaces, and eventually a platform team asking, “Wait, how many of these do we have?”

In five minutes, we’ll look at what the last decade of API and platform engineering can teach us about the next few years of MCP, and which mistakes we really don’t need to make twice.

sessions.title: Upstream First Security: Keeping Telco Infrastructure Secure at Cloud Native Scale
sessions.description:
Telco infrastructure runs on bare metal that powers 5G mobile networks. When a CVE drops in Go dependency used by the stack, we cannot wait until next quarter. Telco regulatory requirements mean patch latency is measured in days. Time from discovery to exploitation has shank from days to hours, we've had to rethink how we work with OS and adopt a strict upstream-first approach.
We maintain bare metal Kubernetes infrastructure by using CNCF projects such as Metal3 and Cluster API. This talk covers how we triage CVEs across a dependency tree spanning 15+ upstream repositories, why we always fix issues upstream first instead of local patches, and how we structure release cadence so that production stays within one minor version of the latest.
We will share numbers, including the time to fix CVEs and the cost of backporting vs. upgrading. We discuss how we automated dependency scanning in multi-repository CNCF project. This are mechanics of keeping infrastructure secure with open source.

sessions.title: Postcards From Tomorrow: Powering the Agentic Era Through Open Source
sessions.description: Cloud native excellence in open-weight model serving, training, and agent usage has arrived in Kubernetes, and cost is driving this imperative. Serving, retraining and refining, and using open weight models like Qwen from model registries like Hugging Face is now easy enough that the entire ecosystem is taking action, driving up density, precision, and performance. This year, every engineer -- and thanks to models, many who work in other roles -- can take advantage of a faster, more cost-effective, and more secure Kubernetes. Opportunities in cloud native AI are driving the entire industry and the community is meeting the moment, reducing dependence on frontier models for their workloads and creating a more independent future with open source. You’ll leave inspired to build your own custom learning loops to power your agents via open source software paired with open weight models.

sessions.title: Code Nobody Wrote: Running Agents You Can't Trust
sessions.description: An agent writes a script, runs it, and moves on. Nobody reviewed it, nobody approved it, and no author ever existed to vouch for it. In 2026 that agent is often running inside a pod on your cluster. To be useful it needs real credentials, and to be productive it runs with no human watching and approving each step. If you deploy agents, then allowing this safely is your responsibility, and how you do it depends on two things. What does the workload need? And who is driving it?

sessions.title: Securing the Agentic Tool Layer: A Runtime Defense Framework for MCP Agent Deployments
sessions.description:
Most LLM safety work guards the user prompt. MCP agents face a different problem: the attack arrives through the tools the agent already trusts. A poisoned tool description, a hidden instruction in a tool response, or a malicious server pulled from a public registry can hijack an agent without ever touching the user.

This session walks through a threat taxonomy built from 80+ techniques catalogued under SAFE-MCP, a Linux Foundation/OpenSSF project, then shows a runtime proxy that validates tool calls and responses inline, with no changes to the agent or server. In red-team testing across five model backends, it cut tool-poisoning success from 74% to under 9% and indirect injection from 47% to under 6%, adding under 120ms per call.

Attendees leave with a concrete defense architecture, the false-positive tradeoffs that matter in production, and what to vet before approving an MCP server for their stack.

sessions.title: Why Post-quantum Authentication Will Break K8s (and How Merkle Trees Fix It)
sessions.description:
The industry is actively working to secure our key exchanges against quantum threats, but what about our identities? As industry leaders update their PQC migration timeline to 2029, the focus is urgently shifting from encryption to the untackled authentication challenge.
Traditional PKIs retrofitted with ML-DSA face crippling performance degradation from massive signatures and compute overhead. So, how do we secure K8s’ internal communication without grinding the control plane to a halt?
In this talk we:
+ detail the reality of (lacking) ML-DSA support across the ecosystem which makes even experimenting with PQC incredibly difficult
+ analyze the critical compute and size bottlenecks introduced by standard ML-DSA signatures with a local PKI and hard numbers
+ explore Merkle Tree Certificates as a high-performance alternative to side-step PQC signature limits
+ demonstrate how to run an MTC PKI locally and map out how K8s can adopt this approach for its internal certificate requirements

sessions.title: Building Governance for Hybrid Architectures for Agentic Systems
sessions.description:
Autonomous AI agents are shifting to dynamic orchestrators that switch between local open-source models and external closed LLMs. When an agent autonomously escalates complex requests to public APIs or falls back to a local model, managing data sovereignty, routing rules, and governance becomes a critical platform engineering hurdle.

This presentation offers an end-to-end traffic governance framework for hybrid agentic loops using CNCF infrastructure. We showcase a declarative architecture using Kuadrant to build a secure AI routing tier. By coupling SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identities with Kuadrant's authorization layer, we ensure external API keys are never exposed and only validated agents can invoke specific model endpoints managed by Kubeflow's KServe. Finally, we demonstrate how guardrails play an important role in governance, ensuring payload verification across both local and cloud-hosted model targets.

sessions.title: Traffic Handling Patterns in the Agentic Era
sessions.description:
As MCP adoption grows, platform teams need more than generic HTTP proxying: they need protocol awareness, policy enforcement, tool-level routing, and safe egress controls for agent traffic. 

This session walks through Envoy’s journey toward native MCP gateway support, including MCP protocol awareness, MCP transcoding, native MCP filters, per-user tool filtering, and integration with policy engines such as Open Policy Agent.

We will cover real-world architecture patterns from Cisco’s use as MCP/LLM gateway, Google’s egress agent gateway traffic policy with an agent registry, and sandbox ambient/local agent gateway deployments, as well the trends in agent mesh.
